content: Hematocrit, also referred to as Ht or HCT, and packed cell volume (PCV) are measurements that indicate the proportion of blood volume occupied by red blood cells (RBCs). In males, the normal hematocrit range is approximately 45 ± 7% (38–52%), while in females, it is 42 ± 5% (37–47%). The packed cell volume can be determined by centrifuging a blood sample. Typically, heparinized blood is placed in a capillary tube (commonly called a microhematocrit tube) and centrifuged at 10,000 revolutions per minute (RPM) for five minutes. This process separates the blood into distinct layers. The PCV is calculated by dividing the volume of packed red blood cells by the total volume of the blood sample. Since a capillary tube is used, the lengths of the layers can be measured to determine the PCV. Modern laboratory equipment calculates hematocrit using an automated analyzer rather than directly measuring it. This is achieved by multiplying the red blood cell count by the mean cell volume (MCV). Hematocrit is slightly more accurate than PCV because PCV includes small amounts of plasma trapped between the red blood cells. An estimated hematocrit percentage can also be derived by multiplying the hemoglobin concentration (in g/dL) by three and omitting the units. Hemoglobin concentration is the parameter commonly used by blood banks. Hematocrit is considered an essential component of a complete blood count (CBC), alongside hemoglobin concentration, white blood cell (WBC) count, and platelet count. Errors in hematocrit measurement can occur under certain circumstances. For example, if blood is inadvertently drawn from the same arm where an intravenous line is infusing packed red blood cells, the hemoglobin measurement will be artificially high because it reflects the transfused fluid (which is predominantly red blood cells) rather than the patient’s diluted serum. In such cases, the hematocrit will also be falsely elevated. Conversely, if blood is drawn from a site proximal to an intravenous line infusing fluids, the sample will be diluted, leading to an artificially low hematocrit. Dehydration in a patient can also result in an elevated hematocrit. Repeating the test after adequate hydration therapy typically yields more reliable results. In mammals, hematocrit is independent of body size. Elevated hematocrit levels can occur in specific conditions. For instance, in dengue fever, where daily full blood counts are performed, a high hematocrit is a warning sign of an increased risk of dengue shock syndrome. Polycythemia vera (PV), a myeloproliferative disorder, is another condition associated with elevated hematocrit. In PV, the bone marrow produces excessive numbers of red blood cells, which is reflected in an overproduction of RBC precursors in the bone marrow, as well as some abnormal forms. This condition is referred to as erythroid hyperplasia. When both RBCs and WBCs are overproduced, it is termed bilineage hyperplasia, and when platelets are also overproduced, it is called trilineage hyperplasia. In PV, elevated serum uric acid levels are often observed, reflecting increased cell turnover and heightened pyridine metabolism. Another myeloproliferative disorder, essential thrombocythemia, primarily involves an elevated platelet count. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and other pulmonary conditions associated with hypoxia can also lead to increased red blood cell production. This response is mediated by elevated erythropoietin levels produced by the kidneys in response to hypoxia. Lowered hematocrit levels can indicate significant hemorrhage, such as in the case of an ectopic pregnancy. The mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and red cell distribution width (RDW) are valuable tools in evaluating a low hematocrit, as they help clinicians determine whether blood loss is chronic or acute. MCV represents the size of red blood cells, while RDW measures the variation in size within the red cell population. A low hematocrit with a low MCV and a high RDW suggests chronic iron-deficient erythropoiesis. In contrast, a low hematocrit with a low MCV and a normal RDW suggests more acute blood loss, such as from a hemorrhage.
